Listen to this article Share Nigeria’s telecommunications industry is facing mounting questions over the quality of its services as 44,678 fibre-optic cable cuts recorded in the first nine months of 2026, compensation to 75 million subscribers and a growing legal battle between operators and lawmakers expose the structural problems undermining network reliability. The crisis is unfolding across several fronts. While telecom operators have approached the Federal High Court in Abuja to challenge the House of Representatives’ investigation into poor network quality, the Senate has opened a separate probe into alleged airtime deductions for failed calls, dropped connections and interrupted conversations. The developments raise questions about whether Nigeria’s existing regulatory framework, infrastructure investment and consumer compensation measures are delivering meaningful improvements to subscribers who continue to experience dropped calls, slow internet speeds, failed transactions and unreliable connectivity. Read also: How SSS intercepted Niger-Nigeria arms pipeline loaded on camels Data from the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) show that operators recorded 44,678 fibre cuts between January and September 2026, with road construction, excavation, vandalism and cable connection problems among the leading causes of infrastructure disruptions. The scale of the damage is significant because fibre-optic networks carry traffic between telecommunications base stations and other critical network infrastructure. A single damaged cable can disrupt connectivity across multiple locations, affecting voice calls, internet services and digital transactions. The NCC has also disclosed that telecom operators compensated approximately 75 million unique subscribers for poor network services under its Consumer Compensation Framework. Nearly three million other subscribers received refunds for failed airtime and data purchases, while the regulator recorded thousands of interventions to address network deficiencies. However, the figures expose a troubling contradiction: millions of subscribers have received compensation, yet poor service remains a recurring consumer complaint. A Bank Needs to Know Who Investment meets infrastructure constraints Gbenga Adebayo, chairman of the Association of Licensed Telecommunications Operators of Nigeria (ALTON), argues that the persistent network problems cannot be attributed solely to operators’ investment decisions or willingness to improve services. In an interview with BusinessDay, Adebayo disclosed that the telecommunications industry had invested more than N4 trillion in infrastructure, including approximately N2.13 trillion in capital expenditure in 2025 and a further N1.86 trillion committed for 2026. He identified unreliable electricity, fibre-optic cable disruptions, insecurity, inconsistent Right-of-Way charges and regulatory bottlenecks as major constraints undermining network performance. According to Adebayo, power-related challenges account for approximately 40 percent of quality-of-service incidents, while fibre cuts and disruptions contribute about 29 percent. Security challenges account for another seven percent. He also disclosed that diesel prices increased from approximately N978 per litre in February to N2,050 in September 2026, raising the cost of powering telecommunications infrastructure. The ALTON chairman acknowledged subscribers’ frustration but argued that network performance depends on an ecosystem involving operators, government institutions, electricity providers, road authorities, security agencies and regulators. He said the industry was not seeking exemption from accountability but an environment where infrastructure investments could translate into improved services. On the NCC’s compensation framework, Adebayo welcomed the regulator’s intervention and described the compensation of more than 75 million subscribers as evidence of its reach. However, he stressed that compensation addresses the consequences of service failures rather than their underlying causes. “The best compensation a subscriber can receive is a reliable network that makes compensation unnecessary,” he said. Adebayo’s position highlights a critical distinction in the industry’s accountability debate: compensating subscribers for poor service does not necessarily mean the infrastructure responsible for the failures has improved. Lawmakers demand direct accountability The disagreement over responsibility has escalated into a constitutional dispute between telecom operators and the House of Representatives. On November 4, ALTON, MTN Nigeria, Airtel Networks, Globacom and Emerging Markets Telecommunication Services, operators of 9mobile/T2 Mobile, filed suit FHC/ABJ/CS/2713/2026 at the Federal High Court in Abuja. The operators are challenging summonses issued by the House Ad Hoc Committee investigating telecommunications service quality. They want the court to determine whether Sections 88 and 89 of the 1999 Constitution empower lawmakers to compel the chief executives of privately licensed operators to account for commercial network performance in matters they argue fall within the NCC’s regulatory jurisdiction. They are also seeking orders restraining the House from enforcing the summonses or issuing arrest warrants against their executives. Adebayo has maintained that the operators are not opposed to legitimate legislative engagement but questioned whether the National Assembly could exercise investigative powers over matters already assigned to a sector-specific regulator. He argued that legislative hearings should focus on removing infrastructure and policy constraints rather than duplicating the NCC’s regulatory responsibilities. “Sanctions alone cannot build fibre networks, provide electricity to base stations, prevent vandalism or facilitate access to infrastructure,” he said. However, lawmakers insist that individual operators must account for the services they provide because they hold separate licences and collect revenue directly from subscribers. During the House committee proceedings, Rep. Sunday Umeha argued that the operators could not rely on ALTON to avoid appearing individually. House spokesperson Akin Rotimi Jr. also questioned the operators’ accountability, highlighting poor coverage in some rural communities and the security implications of connectivity gaps. The House’s position reflects growing concern that network failures have consequences beyond inconvenience, particularly as Nigerians increasingly depend on mobile connectivity for financial transactions, emergency communications and commercial activities. Senate turns attention to subscribers’ money While the House and operators contest the boundaries of legislative oversight, the Senate has shifted attention to the financial cost of poor network services. On November 11, the upper chamber mandated its Committee on Communications to investigate alleged deductions from subscribers’ airtime for failed calls, dropped connections and interrupted conversations. The committee, chaired by senator Ikra Bilbis, is expected to engage the NCC and operators, establish subscribers’ financial losses and submit its findings within four weeks. Senator Tahir Monguno, who sponsored the motion, raised concerns about subscribers repeatedly paying for calls that fail to connect or terminate prematurely. Seconding the motion, Senator Ned Nwoko described the problem as one affecting virtually every telecommunications subscriber. Senate president Godswill Akpabio warned that the chamber could escalate the investigation and summon the communications minister, Bosun Tijani, the NCC leadership and operators if the committee failed to obtain satisfactory explanations. The Senate’s proposed measures include refunds for verifiably failed calls, independent technical audits of billing systems and stronger enforcement of quality-of-service standards. The investigation could expose another dimension of the crisis: the financial burden on subscribers who must repeatedly purchase airtime to complete conversations disrupted by network failures. Read also: Nigeria’s telecom market reclaims 200m lines two years after 70m SIM disconnections Compensation cannot replace reliable networks For the NCC, compensation is part of a broader effort to improve accountability and protect consumers. Aminu Maida, executive vice chairman of the commission, has repeatedly acknowledged that poor service imposes costs that airtime or data credits cannot fully address. Maida disclosed that 75 million subscribers had received compensation, while nearly three million others had been refunded for failed airtime and data transactions. He also reported more than 6,500 network interventions during the year. “Compensation matters, but it cannot recover a lost business opportunity or an important conversation that could not take place, so our priority remains reducing the failures that make it necessary,” Maida said. The regulator has also identified fibre vandalism, equipment theft and damage during road construction as threats to network availability, while pursuing stronger infrastructure protection and coordination with relevant authorities. Yet the continuing complaints raise questions about whether existing enforcement measures are sufficient to compel sustained improvements. The N550 billion class-action suit against MTN at the Sagamu High Court, instituted by Fatokunboh Fagun and others on behalf of subscribers, adds another layer of consumer pressure. The case, marked HCS/261/2025, alleges persistent poor service and related grievances. Ultimately, the dispute is no longer simply about whether operators or regulators should take responsibility for poor network quality. It is about whether the billions invested in infrastructure, regulatory sanctions, subscriber compensation and legislative investigations can produce measurable improvements. The courts will determine the constitutional boundaries of the House’s intervention, while the Senate’s four-week investigation will examine the financial implications of failed calls. But for subscribers, neither a court judgment nor another round of compensation will resolve the underlying problem unless operators can deliver reliable connectivity and regulators can enforce measurable service standards. After 44,678 fibre cuts and compensation reaching 75 million subscribers, the industry’s most pressing test remains whether Nigerians will finally get the reliable telecommunications services they pay for.
